text: Proof. Reductions. For \(G\) as in the second statement, \(\bar G=G/\gamma_5(G)\) is nilpotent with finite abelianization, hence finite; its lower central factors are images of tensor powers of \(\bar G_{ab}\), so \(\bar G\) is a \(3\)-group, and \(D_5(G)\subseteq\gamma_5(G)\) follows from \(D_5(\bar G)=1\) by functoriality. So let \(Q\) be a finite \(3\)-group with \(\gamma_5(Q)=1\) and \(Q/\gamma_2\) of exponent \(3\); we show \(D_5(Q)=1\). Tahara's Theorem 6.1 is stated for any finite group with an \(N\)-series ending at \(H_5=1\) [Tah81, §6, p. 159], so class \(\le3\) needs no separate treatment. We write \(\gamma_3\) and \(\gamma_4\) additively where convenient.

text: Identities. (i) \(\gamma_2/\gamma_3\), \(\gamma_3/\gamma_4\), \(\gamma_4\) are elementary abelian: they are spanned by the values of bilinear maps with one argument in \(Q/\gamma_2\). (ii) \(P\colon Q/\gamma_2\to\gamma_2/\gamma_3\), \(x\mapsto x^3\gamma_3\), and \(\pi\colon\gamma_2/\gamma_3\to\gamma_3/\gamma_4\), \(a\mapsto a^3\gamma_4\), are homomorphisms. (iii) For \(x\in Q\), \(a\in\gamma_2\): \[[x^3,a]=[x,a]^3=[x,a^3],\qquad [a,x^3]=[a,x]^3.\] Indeed, for \(c=[x,a]\in\gamma_3\), \(c^x=c[c,x]\) with \([c,x]\) central, so \([x^3,a]=c^3[c,x]^3=c^3\) as \(\gamma_4\) has exponent \(3\); and \([x,a^3]=c\,c^a c^{a^2}=c^3\) as \([\gamma_3,\gamma_2]=1\). Consequently, if \(a\in\gamma_2\) and \(a^3\in\gamma_4\), then \([x^3,a]=[x,a^3]=1\).

text: Tahara's description. Choose bases of uniqueness: \(x_1,\dots,x_s\) of \(Q/\gamma_2\) such that \(x_1,\dots,x_m\) span a complement of \(\ker P\) and \(x_{m+1},\dots,x_s\) span \(\ker P\) (so \(x_i^3\in\gamma_3\) for \(i>m\)); \(x_{2k}=x_k^3\) for \(k\le m\), completed to a basis \(x_{21},\dots,x_{2t}\) of \(\gamma_2/\gamma_3\). All orders \(d(i),e(k),f(l)\) equal \(3\), and the constants \(b_{ik}\) of \(x_i^3\equiv\prod_k x_{2k}^{b_{ik}}\pmod{\gamma_3}\) are \(b_{ik}=\delta_{ik}\) for \(i\le m\), \(b_{ik}=0\) for \(i>m\). By [Tah81, Thm. 6.1] (checked against the original, pp. 159–161), \(D_5(Q)\) is generated by the elements \[g=\sum_{i<j}u_{ij}[x_i^3,x_j]+\sum_{i,k}v_{ik}\sum_{l>k}b_{il}[x_{2l},x_{2k}]+\sum_{i\le j\le k}w_{ijk}[x_i^3,x_j,x_k]\] for integer families \((u,v,v',w,w',w'')\) satisfying Tahara's conditions (A)–(F) (Tahara writes \(g\) with minus signs; the conditions are homogeneous, so the subgroup is the same). With all orders \(3\) we use: (B) \(\sum_{h>i}u_{ih}b_{hk}-\sum_{h<i}u_{hi}b_{hk}+3v_{ik}+3v'_{ik}=0\); (C) \(3\mid u_{ij}\); (D) \(3v_{ik}-\sum_{h\le i}w_{hii}b_{hk}-\sum_{h>i}w''_{iih}b_{hk}\equiv0\) and, for \(i<j\), \(\sum_{h\le i}w_{hij}b_{hk}+\sum_{i<h\le j}w'_{ihj}b_{hk}+\sum_{h>j}w''_{ijh}b_{hk}\equiv0\pmod3\); (E) \(\sum_kv'_{ik}d_{kl}\equiv{}\)a combination of \(u\)-terms and of terms \(w_{gih}\alpha^{(gh)}_l\), \(w_{ghi}\alpha^{(gh)}_l\), \(w'_{igh}\alpha^{(gh)}_l\pmod 3\), where \(x_{2k}^3\equiv\prod_lx_{3l}^{d_{kl}}\) and \([x_g^3,x_h]\equiv\prod_lx_{3l}^{\alpha^{(gh)}_l}\pmod{\gamma_4}\); (F) \(\sum_iv_{ik}b_{ik}\equiv0\) and \(\sum_iv_{ik}b_{il}+\sum_iv_{il}b_{ik}\equiv0\pmod3\) for \(k<l\). Condition (C) is Tahara's (C) for \(p=3\) and \(d(i)=d(j)\), where \(\binom33=1\) is not divisible by \(3\); for \(p\ge5\) it is empty.

(2) Hence the \(w\)-part vanishes: for \(i\le m\) by (1) and since \(\gamma_4\) has exponent \(3\); for \(i>m\) because \(x_i^3\in\gamma_3\) and \([x_i^3,x_j,x_k]\in\gamma_5=1\). (4) The \(v\)-part equals \(\sum_{k<i\le m}v_{ik}[Y_i,Y_k]\). (5) With \(U\) the skew matrix \(U_{ik}=u'_{ik}\) (\(i<k\)), (B) gives \(v'_{ik}=-v_{ik}-U_{ik}\) for \(k\le m\) and \(v'_{ik}=-v_{ik}\) for \(k>m\); (F) gives \(v_{kk}\equiv0\), \(v_{lk}\equiv-v_{kl}\) for \(k,l\le m\) and \(v_{kl}\equiv0\) for \(k\le m<l\); in (E) all \(w\)-terms vanish modulo \(3\) by (1), since for a distinguished index \(g>m\) we have \(\alpha^{(gh)}\equiv0\). So (E) says that \(a_i=\prod_kx_{2k}^{v'_{ik}}\) satisfies \(a_i^3\in\gamma_4\). With \(M=v+U\) (skew modulo \(3\) on indices \(\le m\)) we get \(a_i\gamma_3=-\rho_i\), \(\rho_i=\sum_{k\le m}M_{ik}Y_k\in\ker\pi\). text: Proof. [Sketch; the case \(a=2\) is written out in Appendix B] For \(a=1\) this is Theorem 6.6; let \(a\ge2\), \(\gamma_5(Q)=1\), and let \(x_s\) have order \(3^a\) modulo \(\gamma_2\). Since \(\Lambda^2(C_{3^a}\times C_3^{s-1})\) has exponent \(3\), the factors \(\gamma_2/\gamma_3\), \(\gamma_3/\gamma_4\), \(\gamma_4\) are still elementary abelian, so identities (i)–(iii) of the proof of Theorem 6.6 hold for all \(x\in Q\), and moreover \([x^{3^n},y]=[x,y]^{3^n}\) for \(n\ge2\). The class \(x_s^{3^a}\gamma_3\) does not depend on the choice of \(x_s\), so there are two cases. If \(x_s^{3^a}\notin\gamma_3\), Tahara's (B) forces \(3\mid u_{is}\), every term involving \(x_s^{3^a}\) vanishes by the identity above, and the proof of Theorem 6.6 goes through. If \(x_s^{3^a}\in\gamma_3\), the coefficients \(u_{is}\) are unrestricted. For \(a\ge3\) all new terms are \(3^a\)-th powers of elements of \(\gamma_3\) and vanish. For \(a=2\), (E) now gives \(\sum_i[x_i^3,r_i]=-\sum_iu_{is}[x_i,x_s]^9\), so the pairing \(\tfrac12\sum_i[x_i^3,r_i]\) cancels, formally, only half of the new term \(\sum_iu_{is}[x_i^9,x_s]\) of \(g\); the remainder is \(\tfrac12[r_s^3,x_s]\) with \(r_s=\prod_ix_i^{3u_{is}}\), and condition (E) for the row \(s\), which sees \(u_{is}\) through (B) with \(d(s)/d(i)=3\), gives \(r_s^3\in\gamma_4\). So \(g=1\) for every admissible family. (This step is not void: there are groups of order \(3^{16}\) with \(x_s^9\in\gamma_3\) and \([x_i^9,x_s]\ne1\) [computer].) Theorem ([paper]). Let \(p\) be odd and \(P\) a finite \(p\)-group of class \(3\) with \(|\gamma_2(P)/\gamma_3(P)|=p^2\) and \(|\gamma_3(P)|=p\). Then \(P^{*\prime\prime}=1\). In particular every immediate descendant of step size \(1\) of \(P\) is metabelian, and \(P\) is rejected by Lemma 6.9.

Proof. \(P''\subseteq\gamma_4(P)=1\), so \(P^{*\prime\prime}\le M\), and as the subgroups \(U\) of index \(p\) in \(M\) intersect trivially it suffices to show \(Q''=1\) for \(Q=P^*/U\). Here \(\gamma_4(Q)\le\langle z\rangle\). If \(z\notin\gamma_2(Q)\), then \(\gamma_2(Q)\cong\gamma_2(P)\) is abelian. If \(z\in\gamma_2(Q)\setminus\gamma_4(Q)\), then \(\gamma_4(Q)=1\) and \(Q''\subseteq\gamma_4(Q)=1\). If \(z\in\gamma_4(Q)\), then \(Q\) has the same factors \(\gamma_2/\gamma_3\), \(\gamma_3/\gamma_4\) as \(P\), and Lemma 6.3 gives \(Q''\subseteq\gamma_5(Q)=1\). (Lemma 6.3 does not apply to \(P^*\) itself, whose lower central factors are larger.)

Remark. • For \(p=2\) the theorem fails: SmallGroup\((64,138)\) has type \((3,2,1)\), while its \(2\)-covering group has order \(2^{13}\), class \(4\) and \(|P^{*\prime\prime}|=2\); likewise SmallGroup\((128,i)\), \(i=522,599,621,1755\), and \(12\) groups of order \(2^8\) [computer]. • Check: the hypothesis holds for \(13\,315\) groups of order \(3^8\) and \(2\,754\) of order \(7^7\), and \(P^{*\prime\prime}=1\) in all of them [computer]. • The theorem does not say that such \(P\) are terminal. Of the \(7\,824\) groups of order \(3^8\), type \((5,2,1)\) and rank \(5\) (SmallGroup\((3^8,i)\), \(1\,387\,558\le i\le1\,395\,381\)), \(190\) have nucleus of order \(3\), e.g. SmallGroup\((81,9)\times3^{1+2}_+\times C_3\), and all of their descendants are metabelian of type \((5,2,1,1)\) [computer]. Theorem 6.12 below says exactly which groups of type \((d,2,1)\) with \(P/\gamma_2\) elementary abelian are nonterminal [paper], and on this block it selects exactly the \(190\) [computer]. Its conditions (N1)–(N3) and (E) alone hold for the \(190\) and also for \(573\) terminal groups; the Jacobi condition (J) separates the two.

Theorem ([paper]; checked on all groups of Remark 6.13 [computer]; D5-6). Let \(p\) be odd and \(P\) a finite \(p\)-group of type \((d,2,1)\) with \(P/\gamma_2(P)\) elementary abelian, and write \([a,b]=a^{-1}b^{-1}ab\). Then \(P\) is nonterminal (it has an immediate descendant, equivalently its nucleus is nontrivial) if and only if (N1) \(|Z(P)\cap\gamma_2(P)|=p^2\), (N2) \(\gamma_2(P)\) is elementary abelian, (N3) \(P^p\le Z(P)\), and (N4) the linear system (E)+(J) below over \(\mathbb F_p\) has a solution with \(c=1\).

To state (N4), assume (N1)–(N3) and choose a generator \(w\) of \(\gamma_3(P)\), elements \(v\in Z(P)\cap\gamma_2(P)\setminus\gamma_3(P)\) and \(u\in\gamma_2(P)\setminus Z(P)\), and generators \(x_1,\dots,x_d\) of \(P\). Then \(\gamma_2(P)=\langle u\rangle\times\langle v\rangle\times\langle w\rangle\), \(x_i^p\in\langle v,w\rangle\), and \[[x_i,x_j]=u^{\omega_1(i,j)}v^{\omega_2(i,j)}w^{\omega_3(i,j)},\qquad x_i^p=v^{\alpha_i}w^{\beta_i},\qquad [u,x_i]=w^{f_i},\] with alternating \(\omega_r\) and \(f\ne0\). The unknowns are \(c,\mu_u,\mu_v\in\mathbb F_p\) and \(\eta,\sigma\in\mathbb F_p^d\); let \(\varepsilon_3=1\) and \(\varepsilon_p=0\) for \(p\ge5\): for all \(1\le i,j\le d\), including \(i=j\), \[\text{(E)}\qquad \alpha_j\eta_i+c\,\beta_jf_i+\mu_u\,\omega_1(i,j)+\mu_v\,\omega_2(i,j)+\varepsilon_p\,c\,f_j^2\,\omega_1(i,j)=0,\] and for all \(1\le i<j<k\le d\), with \((a,b,e)\) running over the cyclic shifts of \((i,j,k)\), \[\text{(J)}\qquad \textstyle\sum_{(a,b,e)}\bigl(\omega_1(a,b)\,\sigma_e+\omega_2(a,b)\,\eta_e+c\,\omega_3(a,b)\,f_e\bigr)=0.\]

Proof. \(P\) has \(p\)-class \(3\), so it is nonterminal if and only if there is a group \(Q\) with a central subgroup \(\langle z\rangle\) of order \(p\), \(Q/\langle z\rangle\cong P\) and \(\gamma_4(Q)\ne1\). In such \(Q\) we have \(\gamma_4(Q)=\langle z\rangle\), \(\gamma_5(Q)=1\), \(Q''=1\) by Lemma 6.3, and \(\gamma_3(Q)\) of exponent \(p\); (N1)–(N3) follow. Write \(A=\gamma_2(Q)\) additively and \(D_xa=[a,x]\): the \(D_x\) commute on \(A\) and products of three of them vanish. Then the Hall–Witt identity becomes \([x,y,t]+[y,t,x]+[t,x,y]=0\) exactly, and its \(z\)-component on generators is (J). Comparing \((x_j^p)^{x_i}\) with \((x_j[x_j,x_i])^p\) gives (E). The unknowns are the exponents of \(z\) in \([v,x_i]=z^{\eta_i}\), \([u,x_i]=w^{f_i}z^{\sigma_i}\), \([w,x_i]=z^{cf_i}\), \(u^p=z^{\mu_u}\), \(v^p=z^{\mu_v}\). Conversely, a solution defines a pc-presentation on \(x_1,\dots,x_d,u,v,w,z\). Its consistency test words differ in the exponent of \(z\) by \(-J\), \(\pm E\) or \(0\), so it is consistent, and the group it defines has \(\gamma_4=\langle z\rangle\ne1\).

Remark. • The check [computer]. For the \(7\,824\) groups of Remark 6.11(3) and for all groups of order \(p^7\), type \((4,2,1)\) and rank \(4\) (i.e. with \(P/\gamma_2\) elementary) with \(p=3,5,7\) (\(932\), \(1\,460\), \(2\,232\) groups), the nucleus was computed in two ways: with ANUPQ, and with GAP's own \(p\)-quotient of \(F/[R,F]R^p\). The two agree, and \(N\ne1\) exactly for the groups satisfying (N1)–(N4): \(190\), \(102\), \(110\), \(118\) groups. For each of these, the pc-presentation of the proof built from the solution was checked to be consistent, with \(\gamma_4\ne1\), and to map onto \(P\); so for these groups sufficiency does not rest on the consistency test. Without the term \(c\,\omega_3f\) in (J) the criterion gives wrong answers both ways: on the block it accepts \(295\) terminal groups and rejects \(13\) nonterminal ones. Code: q136.g, run_q136.sh in compute/magnus. • The system is linear and homogeneous in \((c,\eta,\sigma,\mu_u,\mu_v)\), so (N4) is the solvability of an inhomogeneous linear system. The term with \(\varepsilon_p\) is \(\binom p3[x_j,x_i,x_j,x_j]\), the only place where \(p=3\) differs from \(p\ge5\). Whether (N4) holds does not depend on the choices made, since it is equivalent to nonterminality. • The criterion assumes \(P/\gamma_2\) elementary abelian, i.e. \(d(P)=d\); this implies that \(P\) has \(p\)-class \(3\), but not conversely. It covers all groups of order \(3^8\), type \((5,2,1)\) and rank \(5\), i.e. all possible parents in Theorem 6.14, but not all groups of type \((5,2,1)\): for instance \(M\times(C_9\rtimes C_9)\), with \(M\) of maximal class and order \(81\) and \(C_9\rtimes C_9\) non-abelian, has order \(3^8\), type \((5,2,1)\) and rank \(4\). Groups of type \((d,2,1)\) with \(P/\gamma_2\) not elementary are not treated here.

Theorem ([computer + paper]). \(D_5(Q)=\gamma_5(Q)\) for every \(3\)-group \(Q\) of order at most \(3^9\). Hence \(D_5(G)/\gamma_5(G)\) has no \(3\)-torsion for every finite group \(G\) whose Sylow \(3\)-subgroup has order at most \(3^9\).

Proof. By Theorem 5.4(3) a counterexample \(Q\) of least order has order \(3^8\) or \(3^9\), and Lemma 6.2 applies to it; for order \(3^9\) we may use the result for order \(3^8\). The deduction for \(G\) is as in Theorem 5.4.

Order \(3^8\). Every group is in the SmallGroups library (package sglppow [VLE]). Of the \(1\,396\,077\) groups, \(904\) are non-metabelian of class \(4\); all have rank \(3\) (as they must, Proposition 6.5), \(|Z|=|Q''|=|\gamma_4|=3\) and \(Q/\gamma_2\cong C_3^3\), types \((3,2,2,1)\) (\(889\)) and \((3,3,1,1)\) (\(15\)) [computer]. So Theorem 6.6 gives \(D_5=1\) for all of them. Independently, \(699\) of them have \(z\in Q''\cap M_5\), and for each the truncated Magnus algebra (\(121\) monomials, modulo \(3^{19}\), with the exactness certificate \(3^{18}\Delta\subseteq\Delta^5+3^{19}\)) gives \(z\notin D_5\) [computer].

This is the algebra of Remark 6.4(2). Let \(M=M_1\oplus M_2\oplus M_3\oplus M_4\) over \(\mathbb F_3\) with bases \(M_1=\langle e,k_1,k_2\rangle\), \(M_2=\langle u_1,u_2,\rho\rangle\), \(M_3=\langle t\rangle\), \(M_4=\langle w\rangle\), and the alternating bracket whose nonzero values on pairs of basis elements are, up to antisymmetry, \[\begin{gathered}[e,k_1]=u_1,\quad[e,k_2]=u_2,\quad[k_1,k_2]=\rho,\\ [k_1,u_2]=t,\quad[k_2,u_1]=-t,\quad[e,\rho]=-t,\quad[e,t]=w,\quad[u_1,u_2]=w.\end{gathered}\] It is graded, generated by \(M_1\), of type \((3,3,1,1)\), and \([M_2,M_2]=M_4\ne0\).

Jacobi identity [paper]. The Jacobiator \(J(x,y,z)=[[x,y],z]+[[y,z],x]+[[z,x],y]\) is alternating and trilinear and vanishes in degrees \(\ge5\), so it suffices to check triples of distinct basis elements of total degree \(3\) or \(4\). Degree \(3\): \(J(e,k_1,k_2)=[u_1,k_2]+[\rho,e]+[k_1,u_2]=t+t+t=0\), since \(3=0\) in \(\mathbb F_3\). Degree \(4\), triples \((x,y,z)\) with \(x,y\in M_1\), \(z\in M_2\): as \([k_i,t]=0\) and \([\rho,M_2]=0\), \(J(k_1,k_2,z)=[\rho,z]-[k_1,[k_2,z]]+[k_2,[k_1,z]]=0\) and \(J(e,k_i,z)=[u_i,z]-[e,[k_i,z]]+[k_i,[e,z]]=[u_i,z]-[e,[k_i,z]]\); the last two terms are both \(w\) for \((i,z)=(1,u_2)\), both \(-w\) for \((i,z)=(2,u_1)\), and both \(0\) otherwise. (A machine check of all triples agrees [computer].)

In the notation of the proof of Lemma 6.3, \(\varphi(e)=1\), \(K=\langle k_1,k_2\rangle\), \(u_i=\alpha(e,k_i)\), and \(\alpha(k_1,k_2)=\rho\ne0\) spans the radical of \(\omega\): with \(\dim M_2=3\) the form \(\omega\) may be degenerate, and the step \(\alpha(K,K)=0\) of that proof fails. The Jacobi identity for \((e,k_1,k_2)\), which there gives \(2\,\omega(u_1,u_2)=0\), here reads \(2\,\omega(u_1,u_2)=\beta(e,\rho)\), both sides being \(-1\); with these constants it holds only because \(3t=0\). Taking \([e,\rho]=2t\) instead (the same over \(\mathbb F_3\)) gives such an algebra over \(\mathbb F_p\) for every odd \(p\): then \(J(e,k_1,k_2)=t-2t+t=0\) and both sides above equal \(2\), while the degree-\(4\) triples are unaffected as \([k_i,t]=0\) [paper; a machine check of all triples for \(p=3,5,7,11\) agrees].
